title: Reliable retrieval-augmented generation — evaluation, routing, and the persistent faithfulness gap
summary: Current evidence shows coordinated progress on evaluating and improving citation/factual accuracy in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): high-quality, rubric-based benchmarks and system-level telemetry are emerging alongside methods (task-conditioned routing, multi-tool agents) and stress-testing toolkits. However, a persistent retrieval→generation faithfulness gap remains: good retrieval metrics do not guarantee correct, well-cited generated outputs. Builders should prioritize mixed evaluation (automated telemetry + synthetic stress tests + human rubrics), instrument operational telemetry before architectural changes, and pilot routing/multi-index designs cautiously due to operational trade-offs and security concerns.
highlights: Main signal: Evaluation and system-design work are converging to measure and mitigate citation/factuality failures in RAG, but end-to-end faithfulness still lags retrieval quality.
Top actionable artifacts: ScholarQABench / OpenScholar (doi:10.1038/s41586-025-10072-4), RAGe evaluation harness (arXiv:2605.27445), and ORDER task-conditioned routing (arXiv:2609.17012).
Practical tools to adopt: synthetic stress testing (PRISM — zenodo:22759205) to surface brittle behaviors and CiteRAG (arXiv:2601.14949) to measure citation placement.
Weak but important operational signal: CoRe-DoS (doi:10.1016/j.comnet.2026.112567) reports inference-time DoS threats for RAG (paywalled).
transparencyNote: This briefing was produced only from the supplied paper evidence and the provided trend analysis. Several items are preprints or paywalled and could not be fully verified; readers should consult original papers, code repositories, and license statements before implementing, publishing, or operationalizing recommendations.

topic: Prompt injection defenses for research assistants
title: Prompt injection defenses for research assistants — practical guidance for implementers
summary: Main signal: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) that forces retrieval is a practical, low-cost threat to RAG/agent systems; the strongest reported protections come from layered defense-in-depth combining ingestion/retriever hardening, token-level sanitization (attention-driven where available, rule-based otherwise), and execution-layer gating (isolated planner + verifier). NDSS peer-reviewed work (RENNERVATE) shows precise token-level detection when model internals are available; black-box embedding attacks (arXiv:2601.07072) demonstrate near-100% trigger retrieval in reported setups; PlanGuard-style execution gating stops actionable tool misuse even when earlier layers fail. Builders should prioritize low-cost ingestion controls and rule-based sanitization immediately, reproduce key attacks against their production retriever/embedder, and prototype execution gating for high-risk actions while measuring utility, latency, and maintenance burden.
highlights: Main signal: Retrieval-stage attacks are practical and defense-in-depth reduces end-to-end attack success most effectively (supporting IDs: doi:10.14722/ndss.2026.240394, arXiv:2601.07072, arXiv:2604.10134).
Black-box two-fragment IPI can force retrieval of compact triggers and achieve high downstream ASR in reported experiments (arXiv:2601.07072).
RENNERVATE (NDSS 2026) uses attention-derived token signals for targeted sanitization—high precision but requires access to model internals (doi:10.14722/ndss.2026.240394).
Execution-layer defenses (PlanGuard) separate planning from untrusted context and apply hierarchical verification to block malicious tool calls with low FPR in benchmark tests (arXiv:2604.10134).

Large-scale thesis experiments show a full mitigation stack can reduce ASR from ~40.6% to ~0.2%; rule-based sanitization was the most effective single layer in that evaluation (escholarship:qt8zq0952f).

Readers must verify claims, reproduce attacks and defenses on their production stack, and consult original papers before citation or deployment; several items are preprints or a thesis and need independent reproduction. Licensing and access restrictions for each paper remain as provided by the original sources.

topic: Strength and mobility adaptations in adults
title: Resistance training and range-of-motion adaptations in adults — briefing
summary: Across two open meta-analyses and randomized trials in the supplied evidence set, resistance training (RT) commonly produces measurable improvements in joint range of motion (ROM) in adults. Meta-analyses report moderator signals (intensity, contraction type, trainee status) that may influence effect size. Trial-level data suggest low-volume full–ROM RT can match brief static stretching for posterior-chain flexibility in young active adults, while partial-ROM strategies can yield short-term strength gains with different kinematics. Confidence in precise magnitudes and moderator strength is medium because ROM measures are heterogeneous and one trial’s full text was inaccessible here.
highlights: Main signal: Resistance training typically increases joint range of motion in adults (supported by two open meta-analyses).
Program features (intensity, contraction emphasis, and trainee status) are reported as likely moderators of RT -> ROM effects in both meta-analyses.
One RCT (pmid:42589887) found low-volume full-ROM RT produced sit-and-reach gains comparable to short static stretching in 18–25-year-old active participants.

Partial-/progressive-ROM strength training can produce equivalent short-term 1RM gains to full-ROM training but changes bar kinematics (pmid:41718200); this does not directly indicate passive flexibility improvements.
A clinical RCT in firefighters (pmid:42336366) is reported in metadata to show ROM and strength gains, but the paywalled full text was not available for verification.

I used open-access full texts where available (pmcid:PMC9935664; pmcid:PMC11841725; pmid:41718200; pmid:42589887 appears via PubMed abstract) and relied on supplied metadata for a paywalled trial (pmid:42336366). Confirm numeric pooled estimates, moderator tables, and trial-level statistics by consulting the original full texts before citation, guideline changes, or clinical/program decisions.

title: Efficient small language models — quantization, kernels, and system mitigations
summary: Main signal: Quantization + runtime/kernel availability determine whether small language models (SLMs) can run effectively on local/edge hardware. Two actionable paths emerge: (A) aggressive, format-aware low-bit quantization coupled with fused high-performance kernels (MR-GPTQ + QuTLASS) can unlock large GPU throughput gains where such kernels exist (arXiv:2509.23202); (B) a low-cost, device-profile-driven per-layer ranking (SQNR + roofline) can guide mixed-precision quantization to reduce tuning cost and predict speedups (arXiv:2608.26926). When kernels or device support are unavailable, hybrid/speculative inference (Multi-SPIN) is a practical mitigation to boost token goodput at the system level (arXiv:2608.29618). Recommended immediate action for builders: run a focused 4–8 week pilot reproducing kernels and device profiling on representative targets; for executives: fund the pilot to de-risk procurement and roadmap choices.
highlights: Primary deployment lever: quantization + matching runtime kernels control whether memory savings become usable throughput/latency gains (supported by all three papers).
MR-GPTQ + QuTLASS (arXiv:2509.23202) reports FP4-aware algorithmic fixes and fused GPU kernels with large measured GPU throughput gains on tested NVIDIA cards; portability unproven.
SQNR + roofline per-layer metric (arXiv:2608.26926) is a low-cost approach to rank layers for mixed-precision assignment and predicted device speedups with modest error on the profiled device.

Multi-SPIN (arXiv:2608.29618) offers a hybrid/speculative system design to improve token goodput when full local verification/inference is infeasible, but it depends on server-side verification and network assumptions.

None of the supplied records confirm kernel/license availability or peer review; treat performance claims as device- and workload-specific.

title: Resistance training and range-of-motion adaptations in adults
summary: Across two independent systematic reviews/meta-analyses and three randomized trials in the current evidence set, resistance training (RT) is repeatedly reported to produce measurable improvements in joint range of motion (ROM) in adults. Meta-analyses report moderator analyses implicating program features (intensity, contraction type, trainee status) as likely modifiers. Trial-level evidence includes a recent head-to-head RCT comparing full-ROM RT vs low-volume static stretching in active young adults and clinical/training-specific trials showing ROM gains with RT. Confidence in precise effect sizes, moderator magnitudes, and certainty is medium because most syntheses and trials were examined at abstract/metadata level in this run; retrieve full texts to quantify effects and appraise bias before definitive guidance or protocol changes.
highlights: Main signal: Resistance training commonly increases joint ROM in adults (supported by two meta-analyses and trial reports).
Moderators reported: intensity, contraction type (e.g., eccentric emphasis), and participant training status may change RT -> ROM effects.
Head-to-head trial exists comparing full-ROM RT to low-volume static stretching in active young adults; full-text needed to judge equivalence claims.
Strength-focused ROM manipulations (progressive/partial vs full ROM) can yield similar strength gains but different movement kinematics; this is not direct evidence of passive flexibility change.
Key limitations: heterogeneity of ROM measures and RT protocols, small or population-specific trials, and constrained access to numeric pooled estimates and RoB tables in this run.

title: Wearable sensors for movement analysis — validation-focused briefing
summary: Main supported signal: validations performed in controlled settings (lab/treadmill or camera-based captures) do not reliably translate to free-living wearable measurements without method adaptation or using native IMU endpoints. Evidence from head-to-head comparisons and benchmarked wrist-accelerometer work supports prioritizing free-living validation and consistent reference reporting. Confidence: medium.
highlights: Main signal — lab-to-free-living translation gap: controlled-condition accuracy often overestimates real-world agreement (supporting papers: doi:10.1016/j.gaitpost.2026.110232; doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02528-2; doi:10.1016/j.mlwa.2026.100945).

Markerless multi-camera vs IMU rigs: markerless pipeline compared to a 17-sensor Xsens rig showed suitability for movement-pattern detection but larger absolute-angle disagreements for joint-angle values (doi:10.3390/s26175492).

Benchmarks available: ElderNet + Mobilise‑D TVS provide open benchmarks (MAE, ICC) for wrist-worn accelerometer gait assessments and are practical references for algorithm targets (doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02528-2).

Emerging ML kinetics: LSTM prediction of knee adduction moment (KAM) from a single foot accelerometer is a promising proof-of-concept but is early-stage and treadmill-trained on a small cohort (doi:10.1016/j.mlwa.2026.100945).

title: Efficient small language models — quantization, kernels, and deployment bottlenecks
summary: Main supported signal: quantization remains the primary lever to enable capable small language models (SLMs) for local deployment, but practical deployment is gated by low-level runtime kernels and per-device profiling. Two complementary technical threads appear in the supplied evidence: (1) format-aware algorithm+kernel co-design for FP4 microscaling (MR-GPTQ + QuTLASS) that recovers accuracy and enables GPU throughput gains (arXiv:2509.23202), and (2) a lightweight per-layer importance metric combining normalized SQNR and a roofline throughput proxy to prioritize layerwise mixed-precision (arXiv:2608.26926). A systems-level complement (Multi-SPIN) shows speculative on-device/server drafting can improve token-goodput but does not obviate quantization or kernel requirements (arXiv:2608.29618). Confidence: medium. Key operational implication: verify kernel availability and reproduce device profiling on your target hardware before committing to a quantization format or architecture.
highlights: Main signal: Quantization + kernels + profiling determine whether SLMs run well on-device (support: arXiv:2509.23202, arXiv:2608.26926).
MR-GPTQ proposes FP4 format-aware GPTQ plus fused GPU kernels (QuTLASS) to recover accuracy and realize GPU speedups (arXiv:2509.23202).
Layer importance metric (normalized SQNR + roofline throughput) predicts speed-quality trade-offs and can reduce mixed-precision search (arXiv:2608.26926).
Multi-SPIN frames uplink vs downlink speculative inference for multi-device edge scenarios; useful as a complementary systems optimization (arXiv:2608.29618).
Practical bottleneck: availability, portability, and licensing of fused low-bit kernels and the need to re-profile per-target device.

Implementation artifacts, kernels, and licenses referenced by those papers were not verified here. Verify original papers, code repositories, and licensing before making procurement, implementation, or publication decisions.

title: Efficient small language models — quantization + kernels are the deployment gate
summary: Quantization remains the primary lever for deploying capable small language models (SLMs) in constrained environments. Two complementary, actionable strands appear in the current evidence: (1) format-aware algorithm+kernel work to unlock FP4 (MR-GPTQ; arXiv:2509.23202) that can recover accuracy and yield large GPU throughput gains when FP4 kernels exist, and (2) a profiling-driven layer-prioritization metric (SQNR + roofline; arXiv:2608.26926) that predicts where lowering precision gives the best speed-quality trade-off. System-level speculative/hybrid inference (Multi-SPIN; arXiv:2608.29618) can change end-to-end latency/bandwidth trade-offs but does not remove low-bit kernel or portability constraints. Main operational risk: portability of FP4 and fused kernels to target devices (CPU/ARM/NPUs) and the need to reproduce reported kernels/profiles before productization.
highlights: Main signal: Quantization + runtime/kernels are the decisive bottleneck for practical on-device SLMs (supported by arXiv:2509.23202, arXiv:2608.26926).

MR-GPTQ (arXiv:2509.23202): an FP4-aware GPTQ variant with block-wise Hadamard rotations + fused GPU kernels; improves MXFP4 accuracy toward NVFP4 and shows layer/end-to-end GPU speedups on tested devices.

SQNR + roofline metric (arXiv:2608.26926): a lightweight, profiling-driven layer-importance score that predicted measured speedups with ~4% error in the authors' profiling and helps prioritize per-layer quantization.
Multi-SPIN (arXiv:2608.29618): a speculative multi-device edge scheme improving token goodput by combining on-device drafting with edge verification—useful when network/verifier costs dominate.
Actionable implication: reproduce kernels and profiling on representative target devices before committing to FP4- or layer-selection-based deployment paths.

title: Efficient small language models: quantization, co-design, and the kernel bottleneck
summary: Main signal: recent work converges on two enabling levers for practical local LLM deployment — aggressive low-bit quantization (sub-4-bit / FP4) with format- and layer-aware corrections, and model + runtime co-design to reduce working memory. Quantization algorithm advances (D^2Quant, MR-GPTQ) promise large memory savings but require matching kernels; SmallThinker shows a promising end-to-end co-design (sparse MoE + runtime prefetching) targeted at consumer CPUs. Recommendation: fund a short pilot to validate one quantization method and one co-designed small model on representative hardware before scaling engineering or product commitments.
highlights: Main signal: Quantization + runtime/kernel availability determine whether memory savings translate to usable on-device latency and throughput (supporting: arXiv:2509.23202, arXiv:2602.02546, arXiv:2507.20984).
D^2Quant (arXiv:2602.02546) — weight-only PTQ with Dual-Scale Quantizer and Deviation-Aware Correction aimed at reliable sub-4-bit accuracy retention; promising for CPU/ARM if low-bit kernels exist.
MR-GPTQ (arXiv:2509.23202) — format-aware GPTQ and GPU kernels that recover FP4 accuracy and show accelerator speedups; valuable where FP4-capable GPUs are available.

SmallThinker (arXiv:2507.20984) — model + runtime co-design (sparse MoE, sparse FFN, pre-attention router, NoPE-RoPE) claiming Q4_0 quantized operation on consumer CPUs; treat as actionable but single-paper evidence needing reproduction.
